extracted.intended_audience: general readers and comedy fans interested in industry ethics and celebrity commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Opinion-style guidance and criteria for judging whether comedians should accept paid gigs for events in repressive or controversial jurisdictions (exemplified by the Riyadh Comedy Festival). Focuses on ethical tradeoffs, motivations, and public justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gigs that compromise your moral integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept work that will 'blast chunks out of my soul' — i.e., jobs that force you to betray your personal beliefs or conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patton Oswalt says he turned down lucrative offers when the work would conflict with his values (example: voiceover work for a defense contractor). The framing emphasizes internal moral cost over financial gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't whitewash or legitimize repressive regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Refuse opportunities that effectively 'whitewash' or provide cover/legitimacy for governments with abusive practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes performances at the Riyadh Comedy Festival as participating in a whitewashing of 'evil regimes.' It suggests that appearing can be seen as tacit endorsement, regardless of performers' intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize motivation — large paychecks suggest selling out
rubrics_metrics.description: If the primary reason for participating is money, that motive is ethically suspect and weakens other justifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oswalt observes the 'reason for most of these people... was money.' The piece points to rumored million-dollar paydays as undermining claims of cultural exchange or higher purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of cultural-exchange rationalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that performing will 'bridge divides' or promote cultural exchange should be evaluated for sincerity and plausibility; they may be post-hoc defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill Burr's defense that the experience was 'top three' and would lead to positive things is labeled by Oswalt as not 'passing the smell test.' The article encourages assessing whether such rationales are genuine or self-serving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a clear ethical 'no' over moral equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision to decline should be straightforward rather than a prolonged moral wrestling match; moral clarity is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oswalt says 'It shouldn't even be a moral wrestling match. It should be pretty easy,' advocating for clear refusals when the ethical stakes are obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you accept the money, use it to do genuine good
rubrics_metrics.description: One acceptable course (per Oswalt) is to take the payday but actively use the proceeds for beneficial purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oswalt suggests 'take the money and try to do something good with it,' offering a pragmatic mitigation if one chooses to participate despite ethical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid public rationalizing if you take a controversial gig
rubrics_metrics.description: If you accept a payout for a contentious performance, refrain from public defenses or moralizing explanations that invite criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oswalt's blunt advice — 'Take the money and shut the fuck up' — captures the idea that outspoken justification often backfires and draws further scrutiny.
